## Personal Introduction

When we examine global health statistics, it is easy to overlook the fact that behind every single data point, there is a life. For this task, I decided to examine UNICEF’s statistics on Infant Mortality Rates since it is one of the most tragic and sensitive measures of a country’s overall wellbeing.

I don’t want to just plot numbers here; I want to tell a story about inequality. By linking infant mortality records with macroeconomic indicators such as GDP per capita, I want to investigate a painful question: How much does wealth determine whether the youngest members of society live or die?

### Data Preperation and Quality Checks

So firstly we load data using polars and do some Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) We'll merge the indicator data (Infant Mortality) with the metadata (GDP, Life Expectancy, etc.) on both country code and year.

```{python}
#| label: data-loading
#| echo: true

import polars as pl
import plotnine as p9
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd

# Load the data
indicator_df = pl.read_csv("unicef_indicator_1.csv")
metadata_df = pl.read_csv("unicef_metadata.csv")

# Filter for Total sex and rename columns for clarity
ind_clean = indicator_df.filter(
    pl.col("sex") == "Total"
).select(
    ["country", "alpha_3_code", "time_period", "obs_value"]
).rename({
    "time_period": "year",
    "obs_value": "infant_mortality_rate"
})

# Create a new DataFrame with relevant columns from metadata
meta_clean = metadata_df.select(
    ["alpha_3_code", "year", 
     "Population, total", 
     "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)", 
     "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)"]
).rename({
    "Population, total": "population",
    "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)": "gdp_per_capita",
    "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)": "life_expectancy"
})

# Join the datasets
merged_df = ind_clean.join(
    meta_clean, 
    on=["alpha_3_code", "year"], 
    how="inner"
)

# Convert to pandas for compatibility with plotnine and geopandas
df_pd = merged_df.to_pandas()

# Exploratory Data analysis and have some look on Quality of data for 2020
df_2020 = df_pd[df_pd['year'] == 2020]
missing_gdp = df_2020['gdp_per_capita'].isna().sum()

print("--- Summary for EDA 2020 ---")
print(f"Total countries analyzed: {len(df_2020)}")
print(f"Countries missing GDP data: {missing_gdp}")
print(df_2020[['infant_mortality_rate', 'gdp_per_capita']].describe())
```

As the EDA (below) confirms, the average global infant mortality rate in 2020 stood at around 22.8 deaths per 1,000 live births. But the vast standard deviation (22.2) suggests a highly unequal world.

## A World of Divides: Mapping Mortality

To get a scope of the world, we extract infant mortality rates around the world for 2020.

```{python}
#| label: fig-world-map
#| fig-cap: "Infant Mortality Rate by Country (2020)"

# Load world map data
import urllib.request
import tempfile
import zipfile
import os

url = "https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/110m/cultural/ne_110m_admin_0_countries.zip"
temp_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
zip_path = os.path.join(temp_dir, "ne.zip")
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, zip_path)
with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, 'r') as zip_ref:
    zip_ref.extractall(temp_dir)
world = gpd.read_file(os.path.join(temp_dir, "ne_110m_admin_0_countries.shp"))
world = world.rename(columns={'ADM0_A3': 'iso_a3'})

# Combine map data with our df
world_merged = world.merge(df_2020, left_on='iso_a3', right_on='alpha_3_code', how='left')

# Plot using plotnine
map_plot = (
    p9.ggplot(world_merged)
    + p9.geom_map(p9.aes(fill='infant_mortality_rate'), color='white', size=0.1)
    + p9.scale_fill_cmap(cmap_name='YlOrRd', na_value='lightgrey')
    + p9.theme_minimal()
    + p9.labs(
        title="The Geography of Survival: Infant Mortality (2020)",
        subtitle="Darker shades indicate higher mortality rates",
        fill="Deaths per 1k births"
    )
    + p9.theme(
        figure_size=(10, 6),
        panel_grid=p9.element_blank(),
        axis_text=p9.element_blank(),
        axis_ticks=p9.element_blank(),
        plot_title=p9.element_text(weight='bold', size=14)
    )
)
map_plot
```

The map reveals a tragic truth: The highest rates of infant mortality — the most raw and basic measure of how well societies are doing at keeping their youngest citizens alive — are all but locked in place across Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia. Countries shaded in deep red are alarming, with rates often higher than 70 deaths per 1,000 live births as the global north is largely remained pale.

## The Hardest Hit Nations

Let’s take a closer look at the 15 countries with the highest rates of infant mortality in 2020.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bar-chart
#| fig-cap: "Top 15 Countries by Infant Mortality Rate (2020)"

top_15 = df_2020.nlargest(15, 'infant_mortality_rate').copy()

# Reverse country factor order for plotting
top_15['country'] = pd.Categorical(top_15['country'], categories=top_15['country'][::-1], ordered=True)

bar_plot = (
    p9.ggplot(top_15, p9.aes(x='country', y='infant_mortality_rate', fill='infant_mortality_rate'))
    + p9.geom_col()
    + p9.coord_flip()
    + p9.scale_fill_cmap(cmap_name='YlOrRd')
    + p9.theme_minimal()
    + p9.labs(
        title="Nations in Crisis: Top 15 Highest Mortality Rates",
        x="",
        y="Deaths per 1,000 live births",
        fill="Rate"
    )
    + p9.theme(
        plot_title=p9.element_text(weight='bold'),
        axis_text_y=p9.element_text(weight='bold')
    )
)
bar_plot
```

According to the bar chart, Sierra Leone and the Central African Republic have the highest infant death rates in the world at over 75 deaths per 1000 births. All of the countries listed in this index are located in Africa, presenting the disease as one of the most serious health crises facing these female residents.

## On the gap between GDP and survival

Is there a straightforward relation between a country being rich and having low rates of infant mortality? We plot a scatterplot with linear regression to see the relationship between GDP per capita vs Infant Mortality Rate Annotation of outlier and benchmark countries in the chart for further usefulness

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter-plot
#| fig-cap: "GDP per capita vs Infant Mortality Rate (2020)"

# Creating a sut of annotations with just text
annotations = df_2020[df_2020['country'].isin(['Central African Republic', 'United States', 'India', 'Sierra Leone', 'Luxembourg'])]

scatter_plot = (
    p9.ggplot(df_2020.dropna(subset=['gdp_per_capita', 'infant_mortality_rate']),
              p9.aes(x='gdp_per_capita', y='infant_mortality_rate'))
    + p9.geom_point(alpha=0.5, color='#2c3e50', size=2.5)
    + p9.geom_smooth(method='lm', color='#e74c3c', se=False, linetype='dashed', size=1)
    + p9.geom_text(p9.aes(label='country'), data=annotations, nudge_y=6, size=9, fontstyle='italic', color='black')
    + p9.scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
    + p9.theme_minimal()
    + p9.labs(
        title="The Economic and Health State of Countries: GDP per capita vs. Infant Mortality",
        subtitle="Logarithmic scale applied to GDP. Dashed line shows the linear regression trend.",
        x="GDP per capita (Constant 2015 US$)",
        y="Infant Mortality Rate"
    )
    + p9.theme(
        plot_title=p9.element_text(weight='bold', size=13),
        panel_grid_minor=p9.element_blank()
    )
)
scatter_plot
```

The scatterplot evidently displays the strong negative correlation: when GDP per capita increases, infant mortality rate significantly decreases. This is illustrated by the red dashed linear regression line.

As you can see from the annotations: Countries with a G.D.P. per capita above $50,000 (like the United States and Luxembourg) consistently have infant mortality below 5. In stark contrast, for countries with GDP per capita below $1,000 (such as Central African Republic and Sierra Leone), dependence rates are largely above 70.

## A Note of Hope: Historical Patterns

Last, but certainly not least, let’s have a look at the evolution of infant mortality. Rather than crowding all of the five countries’ historical trends into one chart, I have used faceting to give each country its own individual sub-plot.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-series
#| fig-cap: "Faceted Time-Series (1960 - 2020) of Infant Mortality Trends"

selected_countries = ['United States', 'India', 'Nigeria', 'Brazil', 'Germany']
df_selected = df_pd[df_pd['country'].isin(selected_countries)]

time_series_plot = (
    p9.ggplot(df_selected, p9.aes(x='year', y='infant_mortality_rate', fill='country'))
    + p9.geom_area(alpha=0.4)
    + p9.geom_line(color='black', size=0.7)
    + p9.facet_wrap('~country', ncol=3)
    + p9.theme_light()
    + p9.theme(
        legend_position='none',
        strip_background=p9.element_rect(fill='#2c3e50'),
        strip_text=p9.element_text(color='white', weight='bold'),
        plot_title=p9.element_text(weight='bold', size=13),
        figure_size=(10, 6)
    )
    + p9.labs(
        title="Decades of Progress: Trends in Infant Mortality (1960-2020)",
        x="Year",
        y="Infant Mortality Rate"
    )
)
time_series_plot
```

That means in the examined countries over the last 60 years, infant mortality rates have consistently fallen which you can see easily via a faceted time-series chart exploring a globally positive trend.

For instance, India went from an estimated 160 deaths per 1,000 live births in 1960 to less than 30 by the year 2020. Brazil is experiencing a similarly steep and encouraging drop. But it is, as noted above, still very high; Nigeria’s today is far higher than even the United States or Germany 60 years ago.

## Final Thoughts

This analysis shows how much development matters for child survival. Yet while there has been global progress over the years, significant disparities still exist, especially in low-income parts of the world. Redressing these disparities will demand concerted investment in health care, infrastructure and economic development in poorer countries. Every single data point down on these graphs means thousands of people saved.
